title: How To Handle Misbehaving Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles what to do when a large portion of the class, not just one or two students, is misbehaving at once, arguing that warnings and reminders don't work at that scale. He lays out a nine-step reset process: observe without intervening, stop the activity by signaling for attention, wait in silence, send students back to their seats without lecturing, model the misbehavior that was observed, reteach the correct way to perform the activity, practice it as a class, revisit the same activity within a day or two to confirm the change held, and standardize routines going forward. The underlying argument is that widespread misbehavior usually signals unclear expectations rather than defiance, and the remedy is to return to the beginning and reteach the routine.
points: When most of the class is misbehaving, stop and reset the activity rather than issuing warnings one by one.
Signal for attention, then wait in silence to let the misbehavior "settle" before speaking.
Send students back to their seats and model the correct way to do the activity or transition.
Practice the correct routine as a class before moving on with the day.
Revisit and standardize routines so every recurring activity has a clearly taught procedure.
quotes: The truth is, when more than a few students are misbehaving at the same time, warnings and reminders aren’t going to cut it. To fix the problem, you have to go back to the beginning.
Give yourself 30 seconds or more to upload into your memory the unwanted behavior taking place.
Refrain from lecturing or expressing disappointment. It may make you feel better, but it doesn’t help. The focus now is on doing things the right way.
Modeling how not to behave is a powerful strategy that allows students to view—and really understand—their actions from a different perspective.

One of the keys of effective classroom management is to never move on unless your students are giving you what you want. So the moment you notice your class going off the rails, stop them in their tracks.
